title: Extract ref_map table and perform online schema slimming for control plane
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: The control plane tables currently embed several polymorphic reference columns and free-form JSON blobs that are read frequently by control-plane queries (project lookups, membership checks, and routing logic). These cause wide row widths, poor cache utilization, and unpredictable index selectivity. Several hot queries scan or join on JSONB fields and use ad-hoc where clauses which prevents efficient index usage.

Goal: Reduce row width and improve query performance (target: 30-50% reduction in P95 control-plane read latency for common admin routes and 20-40% reduction in CPU used by index scans) by: 1) extracting polymorphic references into a normalized ref_map table, 2) migrating frequently-read JSON columns to explicit normalized columns where it materially improves selectivity, and 3) creating targeted partial/covering indexes and low-overhead materialized projections for heavy read paths.

Scope & deliverables:
- Create new table control_plane.ref_map (surrogate id, ref_type, ref_key, tenant_id, created_at) and migrate polymorphic refs out of projects, routes, and audit_events.
- Introduce small, explicit columns for high-cardinality attributes currently buried in JSON (e.g., owner_id, visibility_flag, routing_tier) and backfill via online background job.
- Add partial covering indexes tuned for tenant-scoped queries and frequently used predicates (examples in design doc).
- Implement an online backfill worker that performs batched, idempotent row copies and validates checksums before cutover.
- Provide rollback strategies, monitoring dashboards, and automated post-migration query sampling for regression detection.

Migration strategy (high level):
1) Schema deploy: deploy new ref_map table and new nullable columns; update application read path to prefer ref_map but fall back to existing columns (dual-read).
2) Backfill: run idempotent background backfills by tenant in controlled batches; expose per-tenant progress via control-plane metrics.
3) Indexing: incrementally add new partial/covering indexes after a sample of tenants finished backfill to avoid index blowup.
4) Cutover: switch writes to populate ref_map exclusively and deprecate old columns by marking them deprecated in code.
5) Compaction: run final consistency checks, drop old JSON subfields, and run VACUUM/ANALYZE.

Safety & rollback:
- Dual-read/double-write strategy during backfill allows safe rollback: if regression detected, revert code to use legacy JSON field while we investigate.
- Backfill has a dry-run mode and a checksum-verification step to ensure semantic equivalence per-row before marking tenant as migrated.
- All destructive operations require two-step approval and OffPeak window scheduling.

Observability & success criteria:
- Instrumentation: control-plane metrics for backfill progress (rows/sec per tenant), per-route P95 latency, index scan CPU, and cache hit ratio.
- Dashboards: backfill-progress, migration-errors, pre/post-latency comparison, and query-sample heatmap.
- Success: after full rollout for a tenant, the target latency and index-scan CPU reductions should be observed for >=90% of tenants; no more than 0.1% migration-error rate allowed.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Unit and integration tests for ref_map accessor helpers and dual-read paths.
- Migration dry-run against a snapshot dataset in staging (anonymized production clone).
- Canary rollout to 3 low-traffic tenants, measure 48h of telemetry, then expand to steady ramp (10->50->all).

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Whether to use a single global ref_map table partitioned by tenant_id vs per-tenant sharded tables. Initial plan: single partitioned table to simplify queries, reassess after observing index bloat.
- How aggressive to be with normalizing JSON fields; normalize only fields with clear selectivity wins to avoid increasing write amplification.
